impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe class action tolling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, affirming dismissal of breach of contract and Fifth Amendment takings claims brought by a bank holding company that lost assets during the 2008 financial crisis. The court recognized that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in ANZ Securities.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides the government with a strong statute of limitations defense against stale claims arising from the 2008 financial crisis and similar events, giving certainty to the finality of government actions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Banks, financial institutions, and other businesses cannot rely on American Pipe tolling to preserve claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims, meaning potential claimants must independently file within the six-year window regardless of pending class actions.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether copyright infringement damages against the government must be assessed based on the terms of an existing license agreement, and whether the trial court improperly applied the 'book of wisdom' doctrine to assess non-compensatory damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that courts need not defer to existing license agreement terms when assessing copyright infringement damages via a hypothetical negotiation, but vacated the damages award in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' and assessed non-compensatory damages. The case involved the government's unauthorized copying of TETRA® healthcare software used by the DOD and DVA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders retain flexibility in damages models and are not locked into pre-existing license rates when proving infringement damages, potentially enabling larger recoveries.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling constrains the use of hindsight evidence ('book of wisdom') in damages calculations and bars non-compensatory damages against the government, potentially limiting copyright holders' recoveries in government infringement cases.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar invalidity grounds that were not included in a prior IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's estoppel ruling against Valve, holding that the court relied on insufficient evidence for one estopped invalidity ground and failed to adequately account for hindsight bias for the other. The decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel by requiring more rigorous analysis of whether a skilled searcher reasonably could have discovered the prior art references at issue.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a narrower application of IPR estoppel, preserving their ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court litigation even after filing IPR petitions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater difficulty in using IPR estoppel to foreclose invalidity challenges in district court, potentially increasing litigation costs and uncertainty around patent enforcement.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Insulet's trade secret misappropriation claim under the Defend Trade Secrets Act was time-barred where the statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict and district court judgment in favor of Insulet, holding that EOFlow was entitled to judgment as a matter of law because the three-year DTSA statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit. The case involved alleged misappropriation of insulin patch pump trade secrets by former employees hired by a competitor.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation have a strong precedent for enforcing the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations as a complete defense, even after a jury verdict finding misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act swiftly upon discovering or having reason to know of misappropriation; delayed enforcement risks losing the ability to pursue DTSA claims entirely, regardless of the merits.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages models and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating the original jury verdict. The case arose from Ford's development of competing software after licensing Versata's automotive configuration tools.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from broader latitude in presenting damages theories, and breach of contract jury verdicts receive stronger protection from judicial override.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop competing products after licensing third-party software face heightened risk of substantial trade secret damages if broader damages models are admitted at trial.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' between a provisional and non-provisional patent application constituted correction of an obvious typographical error, thereby preserving the earlier priority date.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that the change was not a correction of an obvious typographical error, so the patent could not claim priority from the provisional application. Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (used in Paxlovid®) therefore anticipated all claims. The decision has major implications for pharmaceutical patent drafting and priority claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug companies and competitors benefit from strict enforcement of priority date requirements, making it easier to invalidate patents where the provisional application does not fully support the claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies face significant risk from any discrepancies between provisional and non-provisional applications; even minor drafting errors can result in loss of priority and patent invalidation.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a jury verdict form that asked a single infringement question covering multiple patents required vacatur, and whether the district court erred in its Section 101 analysis of patents directed to wireless building automation systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, holding that the single-question verdict form covering all four asserted patents was improper. The court also vacated the Section 101 ruling on the '495 patent for further Alice step-two analysis, while affirming eligibility for the '887 and '371 patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers gain procedural protections requiring patent-specific verdict questions, preventing bundled verdicts that obscure which patents support liability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents must obtain patent-specific jury findings, increasing trial complexity and the risk that damages judgments will be vacated on procedural grounds.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment claim patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's asserted claims were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285 for attorney's fees. The decision reinforces that data collection and processing claims in the agricultural technology space are vulnerable to Section 101 challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: AgTech companies defending against patent assertions benefit from continued strong application of Alice/Mayo to data collection and processing patents, reducing exposure to infringement claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies holding patents on agricultural data systems face heightened invalidity risk under Section 101, and the remand on exceptionality signals potential exposure to attorney's fees for pursuing ineligible claims.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communications are eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated eligibility for certain patent claims under Section 101 while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed infringement findings, and upheld the damages award and expert testimony. The decision provides important guidance on the eligibility of patents directed to improvements in digital communication standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims directed to specific technical improvements in communications standards (rather than abstract mathematical concepts) can establish eligibility; damages methodology and expert testimony were upheld.
impacts.negativeImplications: Some claims directed to mathematical improvements in signal processing remain vulnerable to Section 101 challenges, creating uncertainty for holders of standards-essential patents.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical patent, and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction barring a generic competitor from launching a competing product to Nuedexta, upholding the district court's claim construction. However, the court vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement, holding that a bond pending appeal must be posted. The decision has immediate commercial impact on pharmaceutical competition.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies can obtain preliminary injunctions to block generic competitors during the remaining patent term, preserving market exclusivity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug companies face injunction risk that can delay market entry, and the bond requirement ruling means patentees must post security, which provides some financial protection for enjoined generics if the injunction is later reversed.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in a pharmaceutical composition patent refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the patent holder was barred from asserting infringement by equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed no infringement, agreeing that the pH claim term should be interpreted at the field-standard measurement temperature rather than at the temperature at which the pharmaceutical formulation is prepared. The court also upheld the bar on asserting the doctrine of equivalents. The ruling affects the scope of patent protection for Actelion's hypertension drug Veletri® against Mylan's generic.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from narrower claim construction of measurement-dependent parameters, facilitating design-around strategies and ANDA filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies may find their patent claims narrowed when measurement conditions are ambiguous, limiting the ability to block generic competition.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade erred in sustaining Commerce's determination that government debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit to a Korean steel manufacturer.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the trial court and reinstated Commerce's original determinations that three debt-to-equity conversions conferred countervailable benefits, rejecting the methodology Commerce adopted under protest after two remands. The decision reinforces Commerce's authority to determine equityworthiness when assessing whether government financial contributions constitute actionable subsidies under the Tariff Act.
impacts.positiveImplications: U.S. domestic steel producers and other industries benefit from stronger enforcement of countervailing duty laws against foreign government subsidies, including debt-to-equity conversions that artificially support foreign competitors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign manufacturers receiving government equity infusions face increased risk of countervailing duties on U.S. imports, and the decision limits their ability to challenge Commerce's subsidy determinations through repeated remands.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner who granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue third parties for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the exclusionary right to sue for infringement possesses sufficient injury-in-fact for Article III standing, even after granting an exclusive license with sublicensing and assignment restrictions. The decision clarifies the standing requirements for patent owners in complex licensing arrangements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring exclusive licenses can preserve standing to enforce their patents independently by retaining the right to sue, providing flexibility in licensing and enforcement strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential jurisdictional defense when patent owners retain enforcement rights in exclusive license agreements, potentially facing suits from both licensors and licensees.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence where an entity that was not a party to the underlying litigation filed IPR petitions on the filing deadline of the actual defendant.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness finding as to challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings, while declining to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR. The case raises significant concerns about third-party IPR petitions filed at the deadline of actual litigation defendants.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders gain stronger protections against potentially coordinated third-party IPR challenges, as the court scrutinized the substantive obviousness analysis more rigorously.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies using IPR as a defensive strategy may face greater uncertainty about whether third-party filings will withstand appellate review, particularly when the timing suggests coordination with litigation defendants.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim terms reciting 'executable program code configured to' should be construed as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), in light of the Federal Circuit's intervening precedent in Dyfan, LLC v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling for the '978 patent and remanded for further proceedings, holding that the intervening Dyfan precedent warranted reconsideration of whether the 'executable program code' limitations invoke Section 112(f). The court affirmed the invalidity of the '638 patent's claim 9 for anticipation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the court's signal that 'executable program code configured to' may not automatically trigger means-plus-function treatment, potentially saving claims from indefiniteness invalidation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers relying on means-plus-function invalidity arguments for software claims face greater uncertainty, as the standard for invoking Section 112(f) continues to evolve.
